title: Creatine kinase
subtitle: Muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis and renal-risk features
summary: Muscle injury, rhabdomyolysis and renal-risk features
introduction: Interpret CK against the laboratory upper limit, muscle mass, exercise, trauma, seizure, medication and renal function. CK can continue rising for hours after injury; repeat testing may be necessary.

rows.name: Raised CK
rows.referenceRange: Rhabdomyolysis often defined as >5 × upper limit of normal or >1,000 U/L
notes: Causes include prolonged immobilisation, crush injury, seizure, hyperthermia, extreme exercise, ischaemia, infection, inflammatory myopathy, statins or toxins. Risk depends on CK trend, creatinine, potassium, phosphate, calcium, hydration and urine output.

rows.name: Marked elevation
rows.referenceRange: CK >5,000 U/L often indicates higher AKI risk
notes: This is not an absolute treatment threshold. AKI and dangerous hyperkalaemia can occur at lower values, particularly with dehydration, sepsis or baseline renal disease.

urgentFindings: Dark urine, oliguria, severe muscle pain/swelling, profound weakness or compartment-type pain.
Raised CK with potassium elevation, creatinine rise, metabolic acidosis or ECG changes.
Hyperthermia, prolonged seizure, crush injury or prolonged immobilisation with systemic illness.
overrides: Use the reporting laboratory’s reference ranges and compare with previous results, symptoms, observations, medication and fluid status.
